column13:
From the options presented through the term, propensity scores appear to be one of the most robust and easy-to-implement means of reducing the potential for confounding when attempting to estimate a causal effect. Based on the skewed nature of the VAS score variable (e.g., median above 70), I wanted to refine the outcome to very high (VAS score >=75) versus lower (VAS score <75) outcome to determine whether there was an effect between recent malaria exposure and more extreme/rarer scores of health-related quality-of-life. However, I think keeping the outcome as dichotomous is still helpful from a clinical/health policy point of view, as understanding if recent malaria exposure causes a per-unit change on a continuous VAS scale may be less informative than understanding if it presents a barrier to experiencing high health-related quality-of-life. 
I think it was key to account for the multidimensionality of SES, however I was unable to recreate the more sophisticated score presented by the original authors. As such, I generated a summative score of various components of SES (running water, internet, car, mobile phone, and education), with higher scores indicating higher SES. Other variables (e.g., electricity, homeownership) were considered, with the final index being selected based on the highest Cronbach alpha (i.e., internal consistency). While the highest Cronbach alpha was still fairly low (0.50), I felt that include this crude composite measure was still preferable to simply including an individual item like education or income. Additionally, log-binomial regression provides an attractive option to directly generate estimates on the RR scale (although, as we discovered, such a feat can be done with a few more steps even with logistic regression! Gone are the days of tyranny under ORs!!!).

column13: To approximate a causal effect while keeping mental well-being as a continuous outcome, I fit a marginal structural linear model using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). First, I estimated a propensity score for receiving 2+ doses versus ≤1 dose as a function of age category, gender, chronic illness, occupation, and income. I then used the resulting ATE weights in a weighted linear regression of the WHO mental well-being score on exposure only. The coefficient for exposure can be interpreted as the average treatment effect (ATE) on the mean mental well-being score, assuming no unmeasured confounding, correct specification of the propensity score model, and positivity.

column16: I chose a linear model with an identity link because my outcome—mental well-being measured by the WHO-5—is continuous, and I wanted to keep the full information in the score instead of dichotomizing it. This lets me interpret the main coefficient as a simple mean difference in WHO-5 points comparing people with 2+ doses to those with 0–1 dose. To move closer to a causal contrast, I also used inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with propensity scores to balance measured confounders between exposure groups and estimate a marginal (population-average) effect. This approach aligns with my research question, limits how much I rely on parametric outcome modeling, and is reasonable as long as the usual assumptions hold (no unmeasured confounding, correct PS model, and positivity).

column12:
I began by using Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) to construct a socioeconomic status (SES) index the way they did in the research paper. This ensured a comprehensive representation of all the socio-economic variables.

I then estimated propensity scores using a logistic regression model and performed 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching with replacement, imposing a caliper of 0.1 to restrict matches to individuals with sufficiently similar propensity scores. 

After matching, I calculated the ATT, by fitting a weighted logistic regression on the matched sample and additionally adjusting for covariates to address any residual imbalance/ confounding.
column13:
For this analysis, I first constructed a socioeconomic status (SES) index using Multiple Correspondence Analysis to reduce multidimensional household indicators into a single concise interpretable measure. 

I then calculated propensity scores using logistic regression and applied 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching with replacement and a caliper of 0.1 to improve covariate balance for the ATT estimand. 

After matching, I calculated the ATT, by fitting a weighted logistic regression on the matched sample and additionally adjusting for covariates to address any residual imbalance/ confounding.

This strategy allowed me to reduce confounding and improve the causal conclusions.
